description: Pathway for ASEAN to achieve significant CO2 emissions reductions by 2050.
pathwayDescription: The ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) acts as the ASEAN energy data center and knowledge hub and produces the ACE ASEAN Energy Outlook providing energy pathways for Southeast Asia. The Carbon Neutral Scenario (CNS) is a normative pathway in which the ASEAN region achieves net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, both in energy and non-energy sectors. This pathway builds on the extensive set of stated and aspirational policies modelled in ACE’s Regional Aspiration Scenario (RAS), introducing further emissions constraints, accelerated low-emissions technology and low-carbon fuels availability, gradual retirement of some coal and gas technologies, and expanded low-emission power generation. It assumes that countries improve their energy efficiency according to their full potential, develop and deploy renewable energy sources according to their individual technical potential, and models capacity additions beyond existing power development plans (PDPs), prioritizing dispatch of renewable energy. The CNS pathway also models widespread adoption of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology, and rapid scale-up of low-carbon fuels. The CNS pathway incorporates least-cost-optimization in its projections.

coreDrivers.policies: Carbon-neutrality measures, stringent efficiency action, fossil retirement and low-carbon technology support drive the CNS transformation.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: A regional carbon-neutrality constraint for 2050 is the defining pathway driver.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Least-cost optimisation and the relative capital costs and O&M costs of new technologies like CCS, nuclear, renewables and energy storage determine the net-zero technology mix.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Average annual Power investment rises from USD 55.8bn in 2023–2030 to USD 371.1bn in 2041–2050. This is driven by increased energy and electricity demand that is met by heavy investments in a wide set of renewables, and by significantly scaling new technologies such as green hydrogen and gas with CCUS.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP growth are a common underlying demand driver across all ACE scenarios and extracted from World Bank and ADB projections.

dependencies.dependency_description: The CNS expands the RAS constraints by a 2050 carbon-neutrality constraint and gradual fossil fuel retirement requirements, which are crucial to the CNS power outcome.
Grid decarbonization (e.g. throught the efficient use of the APG) and regional coordination of new technologies and shared infrastructurem, e.g. for CCS, will require regional regulatory framworks.

Increasing private sector investment will be required to meet the target capacity buildouts, specifically through more PPAs. For technologogies with high upfront costs, such as geothermal, public grants and blended finance schemes could be needed for viability.

Public opinion polls mentioned that show a majority of people support a coal phaseout in ASEAN countries. Introdction of nuclear power generation to the region may may require education for public acceptance.
Very high electrification and energy efficiency require end-user adoption of new technologies, although the CNS pathway does not quantify the willingness-to-pay.

The CNS pathway depends on major power grid expansion of the APG plus hydrogen, CCS and other low-carbon infrastructure. The outcome of this pathway is infeasible without these network updates and additions.
CNS requires commercially deployable CCS, green hydrogen/ammonia production, and tidal power generation, besides a strong scale up of BESS.

Land-use requirements for biofuels are lowest in CNS compared to other ACE pathways, as other RE technologies are more competitive and chosen in the least cost optimization over biofuels. The increased land use requirements for wind and solar do not offset the area saved from decreased biofuel production, leading to a net decrease in land use compared to BAS.

CNS produces the largest fossil-sector decommissioning and job losses, requiring substantial reskilling and transition support, especially mid-transition. The net impacts improve later when more jobs are created in the massive scale up of RE.
